latin.2583: THESIS I. ILLI Confessionis Augustanae Theologi qui Lutherani appellantur, non admittunt vulgatam gratiae divisionem in sufficientem atque efficacem. Idque quoniam una eademque Dei gratia est quae in credentibus operatur, & ab incredulis repellitur. Adeoque, juxta ipsos, illa ipsa gratia quam aspernantur & conculcant increduli & impoenitentes, ex se & in se efficax est, nec debet tantum sufficiens dici opposite ad quandam gratiam efficacem.
latin.2584: II. Quippe docent Deum omnes quibus verbum praedicatur, quantum in ipso est, velle convertere, & eandem omnibus & singulis offerre gratiam: Verum divinae gratiae & spiritui sancto conversionis opus aggredienti multos resistere: ac propterea gratiam effectum suum in illis non sortiri: alios vero divinam gratiam admittere, & non ponere ipsi impedimentum; unde fit ut gratia sit in ipsis efficax, & conversionem actu in illis efficiat. Sed quoniam ex parte Dei eadem gratia est quae Simonem Petrum convertit, & Simonem Magum non convertit, quoniam alter ipsi restitit, alter non restitit, idcirco unam ab alia non putant esse distinguendam.
latin.2585: III. Istud videre est apud Joannem Gerardum Theologum Jenensem tomo secundo tractatu de libero arbitrio capite sexto sectione prima. Concedimus, inquit, sane spiritui sancto conversionis opus aggredienti multos resistere, consilium Dei adversus seipsos spernere, & seipsos vita aeterna indignos judicare, atque hac ratione sua culpa gratiam conversionis a se repellere: sed propterea ipsam gratiam in sufficientem & efficacem dividendam esse negamus, siquidem una eademque Dei gratia est, quae in credentibus operatur, & quae ab incredulis repellitur.
latin.2586: IV. Caeterum ut explicet unde sumatur gratiae Divinae efficacia, observat primo duo extrema cavenda esse; neque enim efficaciam gratiae ad conversionem, tribuendam esse cooperationi voluntatis humanae; nec etiam tribuendam absoluto Dei certos quosdam homines eligentis decreto, sed incedendum via media: quod multi convertuntur & salvantur ad solam gratiam divinam referri debere, quod multi non convertuntur & pereunt, agnoscendum esse ipsorum pereuntium culpa unice fieri: atque in hac pia simplicitate mentem Christianam secure acquiescere posse, etsi ex omnibus difficultatibus non valeret sese expedire.
latin.2587: V. Postea vero ostendere conatur quomodo ista inter se constent, efficaciam gratiae divinae non esse tribuendam cooperationi voluntatis humanae, & tamen ejusdem gratiae efficaciam tribuendam quoque non esse Physicae cuidam Dei actioni, qua determinet voluntatem ad volendum & eligendum bonum, quod illi fuit per gratiam excitantem inspiratum. Sic autem ea de re sententiam suam exponit. In conversionis opere Spiritus Sanctus, inquit, tale invenit subjectum, quod nullas habet ad cooperandum vires, siquidem mens hominis nondum renati est caeca, voluntas aversa ac Deo inimica: hoc igitur omni genere medendi atque auxiliandi gratia agit, ut eum quem convertere vult, ex nolente volentem, ex inimico obedientem faciat: illud vero non fit eo modo, ac si homine nec cogitante, nec cognoscente, vel etiam invito hominem convertat, ipsique vim afferat; sed Spiritus Sanctus donat novas vires, quibus assentiri vocationi possit; nec tamen uno statim momento homini adimit veterem illam libertatem, vel potius miseram servitutem, qua oblatam gratiam repudiare possit. Absit igitur ut dicamus, Spiritus Sancti gratiam in conversione Physica quadam actione determinare voluntatem ad volendum & eligendum bonum. Siquidem patitur Spiritus Sanctus sibi resisti, permittit opus suum impediri, videt multos seipsos conversione, & conversionis fructu, ipsa scilicet vita aeterna indignos judicare. Voluntas igitur in omnibus hominibus est post lapsum: ut autem voluntas velit bonum spirituale, id non habet ex suis viribus, siquidem peccato servit: renovat igitur Spiritus Sanctus in conversione hominis voluntatem, ac donat ei novas vires, quibus instructa bonum actu velle & eligere possit: interim ex adhaerente naturae pravitate potest homo nolle bonum, potest Spiritus Sancti opus impedire: ac proinde neutiquam dicendum, quod in conversione Physica quadam actione gratia determinet voluntatem ad volendum ac eligendum bonum. Quippe hac ratione, ut ait idem Doctor, converterentur omnes immutabili necessitate, quos Spiritus Sanctus converti vult. Quod absurdum ille judicat.
latin.2588: VI. Eandem doctrinam tradit & distinctius explicat Georgius Calixtus, antehac Theologiae in Academia Julia Professor, Epitome Theologiae ex ore dictantis excepta. Ibi enim tractatu de ministerio verbi pagina 241. docet, quando minister verbi legalem & Evangelicam doctrinam hominibus proponit, Deum per hoc suum medium & instrumentum efficacem esse, & in cordibus humanis contritionem de commissis peccatis, fiduciam in meritum Christi, peccatorum odium, novaeque vitae studium excitare, nisi tamen ipsi homines suapte pertinacia & pervicacia tenebras magis diligant quam lucem.
latin.2589: VII. Ex ejus enim sententia, nullum dubium est, quin homo oblatam gratiam spernere, rejicere, & Spiritui Sancto fidem operaturo resistere possit. Quoniam Deus homines absoluta sua potentia non trahit & convertit, verum hoc facit secundum ordinem & modum quem semel instituit. Contra vero certum est, hominem posse solicitum esse de sua salute, posse curam suscipere de mediis ad eam, juxta illud, Multi quaerent intrare & non poterunt. Quippe posse hominem audire verbum Dei, imo cum omni alacritate verbum suscipere & scrutari studio discendae & cognoscendae veritatis.
latin.2590: VIII. Hoc autem qui faciunt, eos Deus, secundum hujus Doctoris mentem, majoribus auxiliis dignatur, ut intelligant verbum, ex eo peccata sua agnoscant, & promissionibus Evangelicis fidem habeant: non quidem quod ista qualiscunque opera tantae sit dignitatis aut meriti, sed quod suo verbo Deus eum velit honorem haberi, hunc ordinem servari, & hoc ab homine praestari, priusquam ipse majora & specialiora, & suo genere supernaturalia suppeditet auxilia.
latin.2591: IX. Distinguit enim author ille inter actiones suo genere supernaturales, id est, quae natura sua vires humanas superant, nec in hominum manu positae sunt, & propterea spiritui sancto sunt ascribendae, quales sunt credere, Deum timere atque diligere, aliaeque similes, quibus constat vera ad Deum conversio: & inter actus quosdam in hominis potestate sitos, quos ab ipso Deus praestari velit, priusquam ad auxilia & dona supernaturalia progressus fiat, saltem quoad modum ordinarium. Quales actus sunt verbum Dei audire, illud scrutari, ad illud attendere, & de mediis ad salutem curam aliquam suscipere.
latin.2592: X. Credere, inquit, actio est suo genere supernaturalis, sive sua natura supra vires humanas, propterea Spiritui Sancto eam ascribimus, quod is animum humanum ad credendum excitet, efficiatque ut homo credat, diligat, Deum timeat, imo ut credere, timere & diligere velit, atque sic actus supernaturales, veramque conversionem ingredientes, sive constituentes Deo tribuimus, & in manu hominum positos negamus: ita tamen ut non negemus esse quosdam in hominis potestate sitos, quos ab ipso Deus praestari velit, priusquam ad auxilia & dona supernaturalia progressus fiat, certe quoad modum ordinarium.
latin.2593: XI. Quibus consona sunt ea quae alibi tradit idem autor. Id autem observandum est, inquit, posito quod Deus Evangelium revelaverit, & passim inter homines praedicari faciat per homines, non esse supra vires naturae quod quis Evangelium audiat, concipiat, consideret, & cum iis quae ab aliis, Judaeis puta vel Mahumetanis, tanquam divinitus revelata proferuntur comparet. In judicio de controversiis Theologicis quae inter Lutheranos & Reformatos agitantur, num. 33.
latin.2594: XII. Itaque juxta ipsum, quicunque verbum audiunt, neque aspernantur consilium Dei in semetipsos, ac verbum Dei non suffocant curis aut divitiis, aut voluptatibus hujus vitae, ii, inquam, Dei opem & operam sentiunt, ejusque gratuita benevolentia ad fidem & vitam deducuntur. Qui vero contra faciunt, suae negligentiae & contumaciae imputare debent, quod a Deo fide non donentur.
latin.2595: XIII. Quanquam autem Dei verbum sit instrumentum quo Deus uti solet in hominum conversione, non tamen vult illos ipsos quibus verbum praedicatum non est, omnibus ad salutem mediis destitui: sed Deum sic se gerere & affectum esse erga ipsos, ut si pereant id fiat propria ipsorum culpa, non quod necessariis auxiliis careant. Quoniam si recte utantur facultatibus & viribus in natura corrupta relictis, Deus paratus est iis prospicere de mediis quibus ad pleniorem cognitionem, adeoque tandem ad veram & salutarem fidem deduci possint.
latin.2596: XIV. Postquam enim hanc sibi quaestionem proposuit, Quomodo ad fidem pervenient, qui neque inter Christianos degunt, neque fando unquam quicquam acceperunt de Christianis; a quibus, scilicet, solis verbum audire datur: annon illi sine ulla suae negligentiae culpa pereunt, ideo quod iis Deus non prospexerit, quo verbum sicut aliae gentes audire possent? Inter alia Respondet, Omnibus hominibus superesse aliquas intellectus & voluntatis vires, & naturales notitias, quibus si qui recte usi fuerint, salutis suae curam habuerint, & de ea quantum possunt laboraverint, iis Deum de mediis prospecturum, quibus ad pleniorem & perfectiorem, adeoque revelationi divinae innixam cognitionem deducantur. Cujus rei exemplum nos habere existimat in Cornelio Centurione, & in Eunucho reginae Candaces.
latin.2597: XV. Quod si autem, inquit, alii horum dissimiles, quae praesto sunt media & auxilia neglexerint, igniculos innatos restinxerint, & veritatem, ut ait Paulus, in injustitia detinuerint, non certe aliquo fato, aut divino decreto, sed propria sua culpa ab illustriore lumine prohibentur. In jam citata Epitome Theologiae pag. 244.
latin.2598: XVI. Porro ex antedictis manifestum est, Augustanae Confessionis Theologos non admittere quidem distinctionem gratiae in sufficientem atque efficacem, quae in Schola Romana plurimum usitata est, sed tamen illud ponere quod per gratiam sufficientem plerique Scholae illius Doctores significatum volunt. Nempe illis qui per praedicationem Evangelii non convertuntur, nullum ex parte Dei deesse auxilium quod ad conversionem ipsorum necessarium sit, & sine quo converti non possint: adeoque incredulis ipsis verbum Dei rejicientibus eam offerri gratiam quae abunde sufficiat illis ad poenitentiam & fidem adducendis, si ea uti non recusent.
latin.2599: XVII. Nec minus evidens est Doctores illos, secundum principia a se posita, non multum laborare ut efficaciam gratiae cum arbitrii humani libertate concilient: quandoquidem statuunt voluntatem ad bonum per gratiam Physice non praedeterminari; nec ullam voluntati per gratiam bene agendi necessitatem imponi: sed hominem libere posse vel gratiae divinae efficaciam admittere, ea per naturam praestando, quae sapientia divina ab eo praeexigit, ut gratia suam in illo efficaciam exerat; vel obicem & impedimentum eidem gratiae ponere, ea negligendo sine quibus gratia in hominem agere non solet, nempe Dei verbum audire, scrutari, atque meditari.
latin.2600: XVIII. Quae est doctrina Georgii Calixti in citato judicio de Controversiis quae inter Lutheranos & Reformatos agitantur numero 32. Ubi postquam constituit Evangelium esse organum divinum ad fidem & salutem hominibus impertiendum destinatum, cum quo per aures ad mentem immisso conjuncta est gratia divina supernaturalis, per quam praestatur, ut homo qui sibi relictus pridem non poterat assensum & fidem praebere jam possit, subjungit, Facultatem itaque credendi, qua destitutus ante erat, consequitur, necessitate tamen nulla astringitur, quia si indoli & pravitati suae fraenos laxat, potest obsistere & obniti Spiritui Sancto, & Verbum Dei repellere ..... Quod itaque homo Evangelium audiens & considerans credat, imo credere possit, acceptum ferendum est, non naturae viribus, sed gratiae cum Evangelio connexae, & per illud suppeditatae: quod autem gratiae possit refragari, congenitae pravitati & indoli imputandum. Quia enim per gratiam quidem suam Deus efficax est & operatur, non tamen potentia absoluta, sed conditiones & ordinem admittente, inde fit quod successu & eventu frustrari possit.
latin.2601: XIX. Neque his repugnat quod dicunt iidem Theologi, conversionem hominis esse unius & solius Spiritus Sancti opus, & hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere. Nec enim per id negare intendunt actus fidei, spei, timoris, & amoris, in quibus vera ad Deum conversio consistit, esse actus vitales ab hominis voluntate libere elicitos, sed hoc, ad actus istos eliciendos; aliosque similes nihil prorsus valere naturales voluntatis vires; nec voluntatem ulla tenus ex naturalibus illis suis viribus gratiae divinae quae hominem convertit cooperari posse, neque illam quicquam ex suo tribuere, quum Spiritus Sanctus per verbum auditum illam immutare atque innovare aggreditur, & novas vires illi sufficere.
latin.2602: XX. Huc redit quod habet liber Concordiae in Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Augustanae confessionis capite de libero arbitrio sub finem. Quod, inquit, Lutherus scripsit, hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere: id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus. Hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem ac regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. Relinquuntur igitur ante conversionem hominis duae tantum efficientes causae ad conversionem efficaces, nimirum Spiritus Sanctus & verbum Dei, quod est instrumentum Spiritus Sancti, quo conversionem hominis efficit. Hoc verbum homo certe audire debet: sed tamen ut illud ipsum vera fide amplectatur, id nequaquam suis viribus propriis, sed sola gratia & operatione Spiritus Sancti obtinere potest.

sections.title: The Lutherans reject the division of grace into sufficient and efficacious
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. THOSE Theologians of the Augsburg Confession who are called Lutherans, do not admit the common division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. And that because one and the same grace of God it is which works in believers, & is repelled by unbelievers. And so, according to them, that very grace which the unbelieving & impenitent spurn & trample on, is of itself & in itself efficacious, nor ought it to be called merely sufficient as opposed to some efficacious grace.
pass_b: Thesis I. The theologians of the Augsburg Confession known as Lutherans reject the familiar division of grace into sufficient and efficacious. Their reason is that the grace of God at work in believers is one and the same as the grace that unbelievers drive away.

On their view, therefore, the very grace that the unbelieving and impenitent scorn and tread underfoot is efficacious of itself and in itself. It should not be called merely sufficient, as if set against some other grace that is efficacious.

sections.title: One grace converts Peter and leaves Simon Magus unconverted
sections.pass_a: II. For they teach that God wills, as far as in him lies, to convert all to whom the word is preached, & offers the same grace to all & each: But that many resist divine grace & the holy spirit when he undertakes the work of conversion: and therefore grace does not obtain its effect in them: but that others admit divine grace, & do not put an impediment to it; whence it comes about that grace is efficacious in them, & actually effects conversion in them. But since on the part of God it is the same grace which converted Simon Peter, & did not convert Simon Magus, because the one resisted it, the other did not resist, therefore they think the one is not to be distinguished from the other.
pass_b: Thesis II. They teach that God, so far as it rests with him, wants to convert everyone to whom the word is preached, and offers the same grace to all and to each. Many, however, resist divine grace and the Holy Spirit as he sets about the work of conversion, so in them grace does not achieve its effect. Others let divine grace in and put no obstacle in its way, and in them grace is efficacious and actually brings about conversion.

Since, on God's side, the grace that converted Simon Peter is the same grace that failed to convert Simon Magus, the difference being only that one resisted and the other did not, they see no reason to distinguish one grace from the other.

sections.title: Gerhard: one grace, worked in believers and repelled by unbelievers
sections.pass_a: III. This may be seen in John Gerhard Theologian of Jena in the second tome in the treatise on free choice chapter six section one. We grant indeed, he says, that many resist the holy spirit undertaking the work of conversion, spurn the counsel of God against themselves, & judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, and in this way by their own fault repel from themselves the grace of conversion: but we deny that on that account grace itself is to be divided into sufficient & efficacious, since one and the same grace of God it is, which works in believers, & which is repelled by unbelievers.
pass_b: Thesis III. This can be found in Johann Gerhard, theologian of Jena, in his second tome, in the treatise on free choice, chapter 6, section 1. 'We readily grant,' he writes, 'that many resist the Holy Spirit as he undertakes the work of conversion, reject God's counsel against themselves, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, so that by their own fault they drive the grace of conversion away from themselves.

Yet we deny that grace itself must for that reason be split into sufficient and efficacious, because the grace of God that works in believers and the grace that unbelievers drive away are one and the same.'

sections.title: Gerhard: two extremes to avoid, and a middle way
sections.pass_a: IV. But to explain whence the efficacy of Divine grace is taken, he observes first that two extremes are to be avoided; for neither is the efficacy of grace for conversion, to be attributed to the cooperation of the human will; nor again to be attributed to an absolute decree of God choosing certain particular men, but one must go by a middle way: that many are converted & saved is to be referred to divine grace alone, that many are not converted & perish, is to be acknowledged to happen solely by the fault of those perishing themselves: and that in this pious simplicity the Christian mind can safely rest, even if it could not extricate itself from all the difficulties.
pass_b: Thesis IV. To explain where the efficacy of divine grace comes from, he first notes two extremes to be avoided. The efficacy of grace for conversion must not be credited to the cooperation of the human will, nor to an absolute decree of God choosing certain particular people. One must take a middle way instead.

That many are converted and saved is to be put down to divine grace alone; that many are not converted and are lost must be recognized as happening only through the fault of those who are lost. In this devout simplicity, he says, a Christian mind can rest secure, even if it cannot find its way out of every difficulty.

sections.title: Gerhard: grace does not determine the will by physical action
sections.pass_a: V. But afterwards he tries to show how these agree together, that the efficacy of divine grace is not to be attributed to the cooperation of the human will, & yet that the efficacy of the same grace is also not to be attributed to some Physical action of God, by which he determines the will to will & choose the good, which was inspired in it through exciting grace. And thus he sets out his opinion on the matter. In the work of conversion the Holy Spirit, he says, finds such a subject, as has no strength for cooperating, since the mind of a man not yet reborn is blind, the will averse and hostile to God: he therefore acts by every kind of healing and helping grace, that him whom he wills to convert, he may make from unwilling willing, from an enemy obedient: but that does not happen in such a way, as if he converted a man without the man thinking, without his knowing, or even against his will, and did violence to him; but the Holy Spirit gives new strength, by which he can assent to the calling; nor yet does he at one single moment take from man that old liberty, or rather wretched slavery, by which he can repudiate the grace offered. Far be it then that we should say, that the grace of the Holy Spirit in conversion determines the will by a kind of Physical action to will & choose the good. Since the Holy Spirit suffers himself to be resisted, permits his work to be hindered, sees many judge themselves unworthy of conversion, & of the fruit of conversion, namely of eternal life itself. The will therefore is in all men after the fall: but that the will should will spiritual good, it does not have from its own strength, since it serves sin: the Holy Spirit therefore renews the will of man in conversion, and gives it new strength, equipped with which it can actually will & choose the good: meanwhile from the adhering depravity of nature man can refuse the good, can hinder the work of the Holy Spirit: and accordingly it is by no means to be said, that in conversion grace determines the will by some Physical action to will and choose the good. For in this way, as the same Doctor says, all would be converted by immutable necessity, whom the Holy Spirit wills to be converted. Which he judges absurd.
pass_b: Thesis V. He then tries to show how two claims fit together: that the efficacy of divine grace is not to be credited to the cooperation of the human will, and yet that it is not to be credited either to some physical action of God that determines the will to will and choose the good which stirring grace has inspired in it. He sets out his view as follows.

'In the work of conversion,' he says, 'the Holy Spirit finds a subject with no strength to cooperate, for the mind of one not yet reborn is blind and the will turned away from God and hostile to him. So the Spirit acts with every kind of healing and helping grace, to turn the one he wants to convert from unwilling to willing, from enemy to obedient. This does not happen as though he converted someone who neither thinks nor knows, or even someone unwilling, by forcing him. Rather, the Holy Spirit gives new strength by which the person can assent to the call, yet does not in one instant take away that old liberty, or better, that wretched slavery, by which he can refuse the grace offered.

We must not say, then, that the grace of the Holy Spirit in conversion determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good. The Holy Spirit allows himself to be resisted, lets his work be hindered, and sees many judge themselves unworthy of conversion and of its fruit, eternal life itself.

After the fall every person has a will, but the will does not have from its own strength the power to will spiritual good, for it is enslaved to sin. In conversion, then, the Holy Spirit renews a person's will and gives it new strength, so equipped that it can actually will and choose the good. Even so, because of the depravity of nature that still clings to him, a person can refuse the good and can obstruct the Spirit's work. So it must not be said that in conversion grace determines the will by some physical action to will and choose the good.' Otherwise, as the same doctor says, all whom the Holy Spirit wants converted would be converted by unchangeable necessity, which he holds to be absurd.

sections.title: Calixtus: God works through the preached word unless men love darkness
sections.pass_a: VI. The same doctrine Georg Calixtus, formerly Professor of Theology in the Julian Academy, teaches & explains more distinctly, in the Epitome of Theology taken down from his dictation. For there in the treatise on the ministry of the word page 241. he teaches, that when the minister of the word sets forth the doctrine of the Law & the Gospel to men, God is efficacious through this his means & instrument, & excites in human hearts contrition for sins committed, trust in the merit of Christ, hatred of sins, and zeal for a new life, unless however men themselves by their own obstinacy & stubbornness love darkness rather than light.
pass_b: Thesis VI. Georg Calixtus, formerly professor of theology at the Academia Julia, teaches the same doctrine and explains it more clearly in his Epitome of Theology, taken down as he dictated it. In the treatise on the ministry of the word, page 241, he teaches that when a minister of the word puts the teaching of the Law and of the Gospel before people, God is at work through this means and instrument of his.

Through it God rouses in human hearts sorrow for sins committed, trust in Christ's merit, hatred of sin, and eagerness for a new life, unless people, through their own stubbornness and obstinacy, love darkness more than light.

sections.title: Calixtus: man can resist grace, yet can care for the means of salvation
sections.pass_a: VII. For in his opinion, there is no doubt, but that man can spurn, reject the grace offered, & resist the Holy Spirit when about to work faith. Because God does not draw & convert men by his absolute power, but does this according to the order & manner which he once instituted. On the other hand it is certain, that man can be solicitous of his salvation, can take care about the means to it, according to that saying, Many will seek to enter & will not be able. For man can hear the word of God, indeed with all eagerness receive the word & search it with zeal for learning & knowing the truth.
pass_b: Thesis VII. On his view there is no doubt that a person can scorn and reject the grace offered and resist the Holy Spirit when he is about to produce faith, since God does not draw and convert people by his absolute power but according to the order and pattern he laid down once for all.

On the other hand, he holds, it is certain that a person can be anxious for his salvation and can take trouble over the means to it, as in the saying, 'Many will seek to enter and will not be able.' A person can hear God's word, and even receive it with all readiness and study it in an effort to learn and come to know the truth.

sections.title: Calixtus: supernatural acts and acts within man's power
sections.pass_a: IX. For that author distinguishes between actions supernatural in their kind, that is, which by their nature surpass human strength, and are not placed in men's hand, & therefore are to be ascribed to the holy spirit, such as are to believe, to fear and love God, and others like them, in which true conversion to God consists: & certain acts placed in man's power, which God wills to be performed by him, before progress is made to supernatural aids & gifts, at least as regards the ordinary manner. Such acts are to hear the word of God, to search it, to attend to it, & to take some care about the means of salvation.
pass_b: Thesis IX. That author draws a distinction. On one side are actions supernatural in kind: they exceed human strength by their nature, are not in human hands, and so must be credited to the Holy Spirit. Believing, fearing and loving God, and the like, in which true conversion to God consists, are of this sort.

On the other side are certain acts within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at least in the ordinary course. Such acts are hearing God's word, studying it, paying attention to it, and taking some care about the means of salvation.

sections.title: Calixtus quoted: believing is supernatural; some prior acts are in man's power
sections.pass_a: X. To believe, he says, is an action supernatural in its kind, or by its nature above human strength, therefore we ascribe it to the Holy Spirit, because he excites the human mind to believe, and brings it about that man believes, loves, fears God, indeed that he wills to believe, to fear & to love, and thus supernatural acts, & those entering into, or constituting true conversion we attribute to God, & deny them placed in men's hand: yet so that we do not deny that there are some placed in man's power, which God wills to be performed by him, before progress is made to supernatural aids & gifts, certainly as regards the ordinary manner.
pass_b: Thesis X. 'Believing,' he writes, 'is an action supernatural in kind, that is, beyond human strength by its nature. We credit it to the Holy Spirit because he rouses the human mind to believe and brings it about that a person believes, loves and fears God, and indeed wants to believe, fear and love.

So we assign to God the supernatural acts that enter into, or make up, true conversion, and we deny that they lie in human hands. We do not deny, however, that some acts lie within a person's power, which God wants him to perform before any advance is made to supernatural aids and gifts, at any rate in the ordinary course.'

sections.title: God provides means even for those who have not heard the word
sections.pass_a: XIII. But although the word of God is the instrument which God is wont to use in the conversion of men, yet he will not have those very ones to whom the word has not been preached, be destitute of all means to salvation: but that God so conducts himself & is so disposed towards them, that if they perish it happens by their own fault, not because they lack necessary aids. Since if they rightly use the faculties & strengths left in corrupt nature, God is ready to provide them with means by which they may be led to fuller knowledge, and so at last to true & saving faith.
pass_b: Thesis XIII. God's word is the instrument he ordinarily uses in converting people, yet Calixtus does not hold that those to whom the word has not been preached are left without any means of salvation. God, he says, so acts toward them and is so disposed that if they are lost it is their own fault, not for want of the aids they needed.

If they make right use of the faculties and powers that remain in fallen nature, God stands ready to supply means by which they can be brought to fuller knowledge and so, in the end, to true and saving faith.

sections.title: Calixtus on those who never hear: Cornelius and the eunuch of Candace
sections.pass_a: XIV. For after he has proposed to himself this question, How will they come to faith, who neither live among Christians, nor have ever by hearsay received anything of the Christians; from whom, namely, alone is it given to hear the word: do they not perish without any fault of their own negligence, because God has not provided for them, that they might hear the word as other nations? Among other things He answers, That there remain to all men some strengths of intellect & will, & natural notions, which if any have rightly used, have had care of their salvation, & have laboured about it as much as they can, God will provide for them means, by which they may be led to a fuller & more perfect, and so to a knowledge resting on divine revelation. Of which matter he thinks we have an example in Cornelius the Centurion, & in the Eunuch of queen Candace.
pass_b: Thesis XIV. He puts this question to himself: 'How will people come to faith who neither live among Christians nor have ever heard a word about Christians, from whom alone one can hear the word? Are they not lost without any carelessness on their part, simply because God did not provide for them to hear the word as other nations do?'

Among other things he replies that 'all people keep some powers of intellect and will and some natural knowledge. If any have used these rightly, cared for their salvation, and worked at it as far as they can, God will provide them with means to bring them to a fuller and more complete knowledge, one that rests on divine revelation.' He finds an example of this in Cornelius the centurion and in the eunuch of Queen Candace.

sections.title: Conclusion: the Lutherans keep what the Roman school means by sufficient grace
sections.pass_a: XVI. Further from what has been said it is manifest, that the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession do not indeed admit the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious, which is very much in use in the Roman School, but yet posit that which most Doctors of that School will have signified by sufficient grace. Namely that to those who are not converted through the preaching of the Gospel, no aid is lacking on the part of God which is necessary for their conversion, & without which they cannot be converted: and so that to the unbelievers themselves rejecting the word of God that grace is offered which abundantly suffices for them to be led to repentance & faith, if they do not refuse to use it.
pass_b: Thesis XVI. It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the theologians of the Augsburg Confession reject the division of grace into sufficient and efficacious, so common in the Roman school, yet affirm what most doctors of that school mean by sufficient grace.

That is: those who are not converted by the preaching of the Gospel lack no aid from God's side that their conversion requires and without which they could not be converted. And so even unbelievers who reject God's word are offered a grace fully enough to bring them to repentance and faith, if they do not refuse to use it.

sections.title: Conclusion: no physical predetermination, so little difficulty over freedom
sections.pass_a: XVII. Nor is it less evident that those Doctors, according to the principles laid down by them, do not labour much to reconcile the efficacy of grace with the liberty of human choice: since they hold that the will is not Physically predetermined to good by grace; nor is any necessity of acting well imposed on the will by grace: but that man freely can either admit the efficacy of divine grace, by performing through nature those things, which divine wisdom prerequires from him, that grace may exert its efficacy in him; or put an obstacle & impediment to the same grace, by neglecting those things without which grace is not wont to act in man, namely to hear the word of God, to search, and to meditate.
pass_b: Thesis XVII. It is just as plain that, given their own principles, these doctors have little trouble reconciling the efficacy of grace with the freedom of human choice. They hold that grace does not physically predetermine the will to good and lays no necessity of acting well upon it.

A person, rather, is free either to let divine grace be efficacious, by doing through nature what divine wisdom requires of him beforehand so that grace may exercise its efficacy in him, or to set a barrier and hindrance in the way of that grace, by neglecting what grace does not usually act without, namely hearing God's word, studying it, and reflecting on it.

sections.title: Calixtus: the power to believe is given, but no necessity
sections.pass_a: XVIII. Which is the doctrine of Georg Calixtus in the cited judgment on the Controversies which are agitated between the Lutherans & the Reformed number 32. Where after he has established that the Gospel is the divine organ destined for imparting faith & salvation to men, with which, sent through the ears to the mind, supernatural divine grace is joined, through which it is brought about, that man who, left to himself, formerly could not give assent & faith now can, he adds, He obtains therefore the faculty of believing, of which he was destitute before, yet he is bound by no necessity, because if he slackens the reins to his disposition & depravity, he can oppose & strive against the Holy Spirit, & repel the Word of God ..... That therefore man hearing & considering the Gospel believes, indeed can believe, is to be credited, not to the strength of nature, but to grace connected with the Gospel, & supplied through it: but that he can resist grace, is to be imputed to inborn depravity & disposition. For because God is efficacious & works through his grace indeed, yet not by absolute power, but admitting conditions & order, hence it comes that he can be frustrated in success & outcome.
pass_b: Thesis XVIII. This is Georg Calixtus's doctrine in the judgment already cited on the controversies in dispute between the Lutherans and the Reformed, number 32. There he first establishes that the Gospel is God's appointed instrument for imparting faith and salvation to people. With it, as it enters the mind through the ears, supernatural divine grace is joined, and through that grace a person who, left to himself, could not before give assent and faith is now able to.

Then he adds: 'He thus gains the power of believing that he lacked before, yet no necessity binds him, for if he gives free rein to his disposition and depravity, he can resist and struggle against the Holy Spirit and drive away the word of God ...

That a person who hears and weighs the Gospel believes, or even can believe, must be credited not to the powers of nature but to the grace bound up with the Gospel and supplied through it. That he can withstand grace must be blamed on his inborn depravity and disposition. Since God is indeed efficacious and at work through his grace, though not by absolute power but by a power that allows for conditions and order, it follows that he can be thwarted in the result and outcome.'

sections.title: Conversion the work of the Spirit alone, without denying vital acts
sections.pass_a: XIX. Nor does it conflict with these that the same Theologians say, that the conversion of man is the work of the Holy Spirit one & alone, & that the will of man in conversion is purely passive. For by this they do not intend to deny that the acts of faith, hope, fear, & love, in which true conversion to God consists, are vital acts freely elicited by man's will, but this, that for eliciting those acts; and others like them the natural strengths of the will avail nothing at all; nor can the will in any degree from those its natural strengths cooperate with the divine grace which converts man, nor contribute anything from its own to it, when the Holy Spirit through the word heard undertakes to change and renew it, & to supply new strength to it.
pass_b: Thesis XIX. None of this conflicts with what the same theologians say: that a person's conversion is the work of the Holy Spirit alone, and that in conversion the human will is purely passive.

They do not mean by this to deny that the acts of faith, hope, fear and love that make up true conversion to God are living acts freely produced by a person's will. They mean that the will's natural powers count for nothing at all toward producing those acts, and others like them. Nor can the will, from those natural powers of its own, cooperate in any way with the divine grace that converts a person, or add anything of its own to it, when the Holy Spirit, through the word heard, sets about changing and renewing the will and supplying it with new strength.

sections.title: The Formula of Concord: the will passive in the kindling of new motions
sections.pass_a: XX. To this comes what the book of Concord has in the Epitome of the articles about which controversies arose among the Theologians of the Augsburg confession in the chapter on free choice near the end. What, it says, Luther wrote, that the will of man in conversion is purely passive: that is rightly & properly to be understood, namely, in respect of divine grace in kindling new motions. That is, it ought to be understood of that, when the spirit of God through the word heard, or through the use of the sacraments, takes hold of the will of man, & works conversion and regeneration in man. For after the Holy Spirit has already worked & effected this very thing, and by his divine power & working alone has changed and renewed the will of man: then truly that new will of man is the instrument & organ of the Holy Spirit, that it may not only apprehend grace, but also cooperate with the Holy Spirit in the works following. There remain therefore before the conversion of man only two efficient causes efficacious for conversion, namely the Holy Spirit & the word of God, which is the instrument of the Holy Spirit, by which he effects the conversion of man. This word man ought certainly to hear: but yet that he may embrace it with true faith, this he can by no means obtain by his own proper strength, but by the grace & working of the Holy Spirit alone.
pass_b: Thesis XX. The Book of Concord comes to the same thing in the Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, toward the end of the chapter on free choice. 'Luther's statement,' it says, 'that in conversion the human will is purely passive must be taken rightly and properly, that is, with respect to divine grace in kindling new impulses. It refers to the moment when the Spirit of God, through the word heard or through the use of the sacraments, lays hold of a person's will and works conversion and new birth in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has worked and accomplished this, and by his divine power and working alone has changed and renewed the person's will, then that new will really is the Holy Spirit's instrument and organ: it not only lays hold of grace but also works together with the Holy Spirit in the deeds that follow.

Before a person's conversion, then, only two efficient causes remain that are effective for conversion: the Holy Spirit, and God's word, the Holy Spirit's instrument by which he brings about conversion. A person must certainly hear this word, but he cannot by any strength of his own manage to embrace it with true faith; that comes only by the grace and working of the Holy Spirit.'
